blogs.title: The Indefinite Investigation: Temporal Limits on Exemption 7(A)'s "Pending" Requirement
blogs.description: This post will analyze the D.C. Circuit's approach to evaluating whether enforcement proceedings remain "pending or reasonably anticipated" under FOIA Exemption 7(A) when significant time has passed between an agency's initial declaration and judicial resolution. The court's treatment of the Bender declaration as an "update" to prior submissions, rather than a standalone justification, raises important questions about how courts should evaluate aging investigations—particularly in the national security context where investigations may legitimately span years or decades. The post will explore the tension between legitimate lengthy counterterrorism investigations, where premature disclosure could genuinely harm law enforcement interests, and concerns that agencies could effectively shield documents indefinitely by claiming investigations remain "ongoing" without ever bringing charges. It will also discuss the practical implications for FOIA requesters facing stale declarations and what burden agencies bear to demonstrate proceedings remain genuinely pending.

blogs.title: Blindfolded Adversaries: The Challenge of Contesting Secret Evidence in FOIA
blogs.description: This post will examine the procedural challenges created by the government's extensive use of ex parte, sealed declarations to justify FOIA withholdings. Farahi highlights a fundamental tension in national security FOIA cases: detailed public explanations of why documents must be withheld could themselves reveal the sensitive information the exemption is designed to protect. Yet allowing agencies to justify withholdings through secret evidence that requesters cannot see or meaningfully challenge raises serious due process concerns. The post will analyze the court's response to Farahi's objection that he was handicapped by not knowing the contents of the sealed declarations, the inherent limitations on adversarial testing when key evidence is hidden from one party, and whether current procedural safeguards—including judicial in camera review—adequately protect requesters' interests while preserving legitimate secrecy.

blogs.title: Beyond Words: What Counts as "Meaningful Information" Under FOIA's Segregability Requirement
blogs.description: This post will explore the D.C. Circuit's segregability analysis and its reaffirmation that FOIA's focus is on "information" rather than isolated "words." The court's holding that even if individual words or phrases could be disclosed without harm, no "meaningful information" was reasonably segregable from Farahi's 10,750 pages of records illustrates a significant limitation on agencies' obligations to release non-exempt portions. The post will examine the "inextricably intertwined" doctrine as applied in complex law enforcement files, how courts evaluate whether non-exempt material interspersed throughout exempt documents constitutes "reasonably segregable" information, and the practical implications for requesters seeking records from terrorism investigations where sources, methods, and investigative details may be scattered throughout documents.

blogs.title: The Deference Dilemma: Judicial Review of National Security FOIA Claims
blogs.description: This post will analyze the broader doctrine of deference to executive branch determinations in FOIA cases implicating national security, as exemplified by the D.C. Circuit's approach in Farahi. The court emphasized that deference to the FBI is "particularly appropriate for records implicating national security" and cited precedent "consistently reiterating the principle of deference to the executive in the FOIA context when national security concerns are implicated." The post will examine the theoretical justifications for such deference, its practical effects on the government's burden of proof under FOIA, and the ongoing tension between meaningful judicial review and respect for executive expertise in sensitive matters. It will also consider whether the court's approach effectively transforms the government's burden into a pro forma requirement in national security cases.
